title: Effect 4.0 Ships: Dependency-Free Rewrite with 5x Smaller Bundles and Long-Term Support
gist: Effect 4.0, a from-scratch rewrite of the TypeScript framework's fiber runtime released 30 September 2026, claims 5x smaller bundles, 86% less heap for 50,000 fibers and ~6.4x higher throughput (team figures, not independently reproduced), consolidates platform/rpc/cluster into the core package with zero runtime dependencies, and introduces LTS through at least September 2029.

insights.claim: Effect 4.0 rewrites the TypeScript framework's fiber runtime from scratch, shrinking a minimal Effect+Stream+Schema program from 35.6 kB to 7.1 kB, a 5x reduction, per the team's own figures.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Smaller bundles make Effect more viable for frontend use, widening its addressable adoption.

insights.claim: Effect 4.0 cuts heap used by 50,000 fibers from 157.5 MB to 21.8 MB (86%) and raises concurrent throughput from 0.71 million to 4.57 million tasks per second (~6.4x), but these team benchmarks have not been independently reproduced.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Treat vendor benchmark claims cautiously until reproduced.

insights.claim: Effect 4.0 folds core modules from @effect/platform, @effect/rpc and @effect/cluster into the main effect package, puts all @effect/* packages on a single version, and ships with zero runtime dependencies after replacing pg with a native PgProtocol client.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Zero-dependency cores reduce supply-chain risk, a selling point for enterprise TypeScript adoption.
insights.locator: Alongside the rewrite, the ecosystem has been consolidated.

insights.claim: Effect 4.x gets bug fixes until September 2029 or one year after 5.0 ships, and security fixes until September 2029 or two years after 5.0, whichever is later.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: An LTS policy signals the project is courting enterprise production use.
insights.locator: With 4.0, the team has introduced a long-term support policy.

insights.claim: The 43.9 million weekly downloads cited at Effect 4.0's launch cover the whole ecosystem across beta and RC tags, while stable 4.0 itself recorded about 150,000 downloads on its first day.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Headline adoption metrics for open-source launches can be inflated by aggregation; check the denominator.

insights.claim: Effect's team admitted several modules intended as unstable shipped in 4.0 without a @stability tag, implicitly promising stability; every exported API now declares its stability explicitly, and HTTP, SQL, RPC and AI spans moved to OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Native OpenTelemetry alignment fits the broader observability-standardization trend.
insights.locator: The team's own Effect 4.0: The First Week post

insights.claim: Effect 4.1, released 20 October 2026, added effect/crypto modules, a Glob module on Node, Bun and Deno, a streaming Csv module, and RFC 9457 Problem Details support in HttpApi.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Rapid follow-up cadence suggests an active maintainer team.

insights.claim: The Effect team suggests coding agents can handle most of the mechanical work of migrating from 3.x to 4.x.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Framework vendors are leaning on AI coding agents to lower major-version migration costs.

insights.claim: Effect occupies territory similar to ZIO in Scala, alongside TypeScript libraries like Effection 4.0 that target structured concurrency with a smaller surface.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Typed-effect/structured-concurrency is a growing niche in the TypeScript ecosystem.
insights.locator: Effect sits in similar territory to ZIO
